Memory Storage Architecture — Upstream Intention vs Upstream Today vs Fork Today

Status: Reference document, 2026-05-13 Purpose: Three-way visual comparison of (1) upstream's documented intention and roadmap, (2) upstream as actually shipped today (verified against ruvnet/agentdb HEAD a478ab3), and (3) the fork's current state. Informs [[ADR-0179]], [[ADR-0177]] (proposed pivot to upstream's RVF-first vision), and the round-2 council's Option Z recommendation. Related: [[ADR-0179-council-r1-bridge-deletion]], [[ADR-0179-council-r2-axis-architecture]], [[ADR-0177-adopt-upstream-agentdb-rvf-vision]] Primary sources: ADR-0177's 9-agent audit of upstream ruvnet/agentdb (2026-05-12); upstream ruvnet/agentdb/README.md + docs/adrs/ADR-002 through ADR-010; ADR-0067 (original vision controller wiring); ADR-0039 (upstream controller integration roadmap).

TL;DR — three architectures, three pictures

Lens Architecture
Upstream intention Single-file .rvf "Cognitive Container" — vectors, indexes, learning state, audit trail in one file. RVF-first substrate. Two MCP surfaces (memory_* + 18 agentdb_* controller tools), both routed through a coordination layer (the bridge) into ONE store. No pgvector. ADR-005's 6 self-learning components wired into RvfBackend per ADR-006 (default-on, +36% feedback gain). 5-phase capability roadmap targets ~95% @ruvector coverage in 16 weeks (ADR-007).
Upstream today RVF substrate is shipped (src/backends/factory.ts:166 returns RvfBackend). Both MCP surfaces are shipped (memory-tools.ts + agentdb-tools.ts — 18 agentdb_* tools routed through memory-bridge.ts). The 6 self-learning components all exist (~2,841 LoC). The wrapper that composes them (SelfLearningRvfBackend) exists (487 LoC) — but is orphaned: factory returns bare RvfBackend, not the wrapper. Aggregate ADR implementation: ~60%. README's "+36% from feedback alone" claim cannot be delivered by default install. ADR-009 is a 6-byte placeholder file ("i weds"). Both MCP surfaces land in one file (.swarm/memory.db) via the bridge.
Fork today Same two MCP surfaces as upstream (memory_* + agentdb_*). Two physical files: memory_* writes to .claude-flow/memory.rvf, agentdb_* writes to .swarm/memory.db (substrate-split). Native NAPI HNSW on the vector hot path. But: two of everything (backup, restore, audit, init), cross-cutting features have no home (round 1 found 6 features lost in ADR-0085's bridge deletion), ADR-0112 forbids cross-store coordination by design (this is the binding rule that diverges fork from upstream). ADR-0086 ("Single Storage Abstraction") title contradicts outcome (Debt 15 dual-backend). ADR-0177 (proposed, 2026-05-12) supersedes ADR-0170/0174/0175 to pivot back to upstream's single-substrate model, keeping both MCP surfaces.

Key observation (corrected — earlier drafts of this doc were wrong): the divergence is NOT the MCP surface count. Upstream has had memory_* AND agentdb_* since ADR-0053 (verified — 18 agentdb_* tools in ruvnet/ruflo/v3/@claude-flow/cli/src/mcp-tools/agentdb-tools.ts). The actual divergence is one layer lower:

Layer Upstream Fork Divergence
MCP surfaces 2 (memory_* + agentdb_*) 2 (memory_* + agentdb_*) None — same surfaces
Substrate count 1 (.swarm/memory.db) 2 (memory.rvf + .swarm/memory.db) Fork added a second physical file
Cross-tool coordination Allowed (via bridge) Forbidden (ADR-0112) Fork added the no-coordination rule
Self-learning wrapper as default No (orphaned at factory) No (inherits the orphan) — fork commit 511b7d3 fixes it Fork is one fix ahead

ADR-0177 proposes reverting the substrate divergence: keep both MCP surfaces, route both to a single RVF substrate, retire ADR-0112's no-coordination rule, deliver the +36% wrapper fix. ADR-0179 round-2 council endorsed the equivalent direction (Option Z) via 6-of-8.

Additional findings worth flagging upfront:

  • The "150-12,500× speedup" routinely cited for the fork's RVF over upstream is RVF NAPI HNSW vs sql.js cosine-over-JSON (the upstream fallback path). Against upstream's actual primary path (RVF native HNSW today), the honest comparator is 2-3×. No benchmark of the honest comparator has been run.
  • Option Z is a SUBSTRATE collapse, not a SURFACE collapse. Both memory_* and agentdb_* MCP surfaces stay — they're upstream design and load-bearing for skills (adr-index, working-council, etc.). What changes: the substrate that backs them.

Explain it to me like I am 15

Imagine the agent has a notebook. Two things go in it: facts (short text snippets with a meaning fingerprint called an "embedding") and structured records (skill descriptions, episode logs, causal chains — relational stuff with columns and joins).

The argument is about how to organize that notebook.

Upstream's pitch: "One notebook." A single binary file called .rvf that holds vectors, indexes, learning state, and an audit trail. You write to one place, you read from one place, you back up one file. Inside, there's a smart wrapper that watches every search, learns from what you click on, and gets better over time (the "+36% feedback gain"). One file. One API. Simple.

Upstream's reality: They built the smart wrapper. They put it in the codebase. Then they couldn't flip the switch that turns it on. Not because they forgot — because of how their governance works. Their own design doc (ADR-006) says the wrapper should be on by default. But that ADR has been in "Proposed" status since 2026-02-17 — three months as of our audit. Until someone moves it to "Accepted," nobody flips the factory function. There's no PR proposing the change. The wrapper code is in the repo but isn't exported, isn't tested as the default, isn't reachable from any caller. Our ADR-0177 calls this an "unfinished governance handoff" — design intent didn't make the trip to deployed default.

Heads up — common misconception: upstream ships two MCP tool families too (memory_* AND agentdb_* — 18 controller tools like agentdb_hierarchical-store, agentdb_session-start, agentdb_causal-edge). This was the case all along (since ADR-0053). The fork didn't invent the dual surface. So when this doc says "fork has two surfaces and upstream has one" — that was wrong. Both have two.

What the fork actually did differently: upstream routes both surfaces through ONE notebook (one file: .swarm/memory.db) via the bridge. The fork split that into TWO notebooks — one for each surface. memory_* writes to .claude-flow/memory.rvf (fast native RVF), agentdb_* writes to .swarm/memory.db. Then it wrote a rule (ADR-0112) saying "no tool can write to both notebooks."

So the divergence is:

  1. Substrate count: upstream 1 file, fork 2 files.
  2. Coordination rule: upstream allows the bridge to coordinate writes across tool families; fork forbids it.

That's it. Both have the same MCP tool surface. The fork moved the storage layer apart and wrote a rule saying it stays apart.

The cost of splitting the substrate (not the surface):

  • Two files to back up. Two files to restore. Two files to lose if your disk has a bad day.
  • Some features (audit log, write-validation, fancy search-result-explanations) only make sense as cross-cutting — they apply to every write regardless of which substrate it lands on. With one substrate, there's one obvious place to put them. With two, you either put them in both (doubling code) or pick one (leaving the other unguarded).
  • When you ask "what did Agent X do today?", you have to query two logs and merge them by timestamp — and the timestamps might be slightly off because each file has its own clock-and-sync rules.
  • Six features the deleted bridge was holding (think "guard rails on the write API") got lost because they didn't have a home in either substrate. We're now restoring them (ADR-0179), but as two sets of guard rails — one per substrate.

The bug we already fixed but upstream hasn't: The orphaned smart wrapper. We flipped the factory ourselves on the fork's side (forks/agentdb commit 511b7d3, 2026-05-12). Three-line change: import the wrapper type, return SelfLearningRvfBackend.create() instead of new RvfBackend(). Once verified by npm run release acceptance + NDCG@10 benchmark, the fork's @sparkleideas/agentdb delivers the +36% feedback gain upstream advertises but doesn't run.

Why don't we just send the fix back to upstream? We could (it would be a one-line PR citing upstream's own ADR-006 — hard to argue against a project's own ADR). But our project rule (memory: feedback-no-upstream-donate-backs) says fork improvements stay fork-only. We documented the rationale in ADR-0177 Phase 7 and retired the PR plan. The fix lives in the fork; upstream remains stuck at "Proposed" until upstream's maintainer chooses to flip ADR-006 to "Accepted."

What's stopping us from completing the rest of upstream's "Cognitive Container" vision? Upstream has a 5-phase, 16-week roadmap (ADR-007) to reach 95% capability coverage. Our 9-agent audit measured upstream at ~60% aggregate. The remaining 35% breaks down honestly:

  • ~5% is fork-doable in days — init wizards, the missing 7 agentdb_rvf_* MCP tools, doctor RVF availability checks, three minor SoTA enhancements to the self-learning wrapper (DPO loss, NV-Retriever false-negative filter, SCAFFOLD/K-Merge federation).
  • ~20% is genuinely big features — kernel embedding APIs, eBPF compute hooks, streaming graph events, RuvLLM engine integration, full SafeTensors/HF model import/export pipeline. Multi-week scope each. Fork picks high-value pieces when they earn the engineering time.
  • ~10% is upstream-only or impossible: a chat UI package (ADR-008) that doesn't exist yet, and ADR-009 which is literally a 6-byte placeholder file containing the text "i weds" — no design to implement.

So the gap isn't "we forgot" or "we don't know how." It's three different kinds of friction stacking up:

  1. Governance friction at upstream (ADR-006 status flip) → blocks the +36% loop for default installs but is ALREADY worked around in the fork.
  2. Scope vs effort at ~20% of the audit gap → big features that need real engineering investment.
  3. Upstream artifacts that don't exist or aren't designed → can't be completed by anyone, fork or upstream.

The fork ships ~60% of the audit baseline + targeted fork-only improvements (factory flip, Cypher executor patch, embedding config through ruflo's config chain). We're paced by engineering economics, not by knowledge gaps.

What the council recommended (Option Z, corrected framing): keep BOTH MCP tool families (they're upstream's design — fine), but collapse the storage back to ONE substrate (per ADR-0177, use RVF as upstream intended). Retire ADR-0112's no-coordination rule so the bridge (or its successor) can wire the cross-cutting features uniformly. From the outside, both surfaces still exist — skills that use agentdb_hierarchical-store keep working. From the inside, there's one substrate, one backup target, one audit log, one place to put MutationGuard. This is what upstream already does at the substrate level (1 file), and what ADR-0177 Phase 1 is already pulling the fork toward.

That's the whole story. Three architectures (intention, today-upstream, today-fork) and one proposal (Z = revert the substrate split, keep the surfaces) to converge them.

Scope and definitions

Three concepts are kept distinct throughout:

  • MCP surface — the tool family the caller invokes (memory_* vs agentdb_*). User-facing contract.
  • Substrate — the actual storage engine that holds bytes on disk (RVF binary file, SQLite database file). Implementation.
  • Vector backend — the ANN index implementation (@ruvector/rvf-node native HNSW, @ruvector/core native HNSW, HNSWLib JS fallback). May be co-located with the substrate or separate.

The fork has diverged from upstream on all three axes; this document maps the divergence.

1. Upstream's documented intention and roadmap

This is what upstream says the architecture is supposed to be — sourced from the live ruvnet/agentdb README, ADRs 002 through 010, and ruvnet/RuVector ADR-029. ADR-0177's references-upstream block lists all 11 source documents consulted on 2026-05-12 against live GitHub HEAD a478ab3.

1.1 The "Cognitive Container" vision

Upstream README (ruvnet/agentdb/README.md:15-19):

"Vector memory that gets smarter every time your agent uses it."

"A single-file cognitive container — vectors, indexes, learning state, and a cryptographic audit trail in one .rvf."

This is one substrate, one file, one surface. No agentdb_* MCP family separate from memory_*; no second physical file; no axis split exposed to callers. The "cognitive container" framing makes vector index, relational metadata, learning state, and audit trail all aspects of a single self-describing artifact.

1.2 Upstream ADR-006 — the no-pgvector mandate

Upstream ADR-006-unified-self-learning-rvf-integration.md:201-242 is explicit:

"Storage Backend: @ruvector (NOT pgvector)"

"All vector persistence in the RVF stack uses the @ruvector ecosystem exclusively. The system MUST NOT use pgvector for any vector storage, indexing, or search operations."

"PostgreSQL persistence: When relational persistence is required (e.g., metadata, session state, audit logs), the system uses @ruvector/rvf file-based stores or future @ruvector PostgreSQL extensions — never pgvector."

"Any future PostgreSQL integration MUST use @ruvector's native extension that reads/writes .rvf segments directly, preserving witness chains, lineage tracking, and segment signing."

This carries weight for the fork: anywhere the fork uses postgres-as-vector-store (including ADR-0174/0175's ruvector-postgres direction), it violates upstream's mandate. ADR-0177 makes this the load-bearing reason for its supersession of ADR-0170/0174/0175.

1.3 Upstream's 5-phase roadmap (ADR-007)

Upstream ADR-007-ruvector-full-capability-integration.md lays out a 16-week, 5-phase plan to reach ~95% @ruvector capability coverage from ~30% baseline, all atop the RVF substrate:

Phase Weeks Goal
Phase 1 — Critical Path 1-3 Native optimizers (AdamW, InfoNCE), full SIMD surface, WASM verification, RVF compression profiles (Scalar/Product/Binary/Half — 4-32× memory reduction), Graph Transactions + Cypher via querySync, router persistence, SONA context enrichment, batch operations, tensor compression, read-only access + filter expressions
Phase 2 — Kernel Runtimes 4-6 Kernel + eBPF embedding APIs (RVF as "active compute container"), model import/export (SafeTensors/HF/JSON), WASM in-memory store, ReasoningBank integration, RLM controller for RAG
Phase 3 — Advanced Features 7-10 TrainingPipeline, segment-signing, temporal-hyperedges, dataset-exporter, GraphRoPeAttention, differentiableSearch
Phase 4 — Streaming + Graph Events 11-13 Streaming token generation, streaming graph queries + subscriptions, hyperbolic attention
Phase 5 — Full Ecosystem 14-16 RuvLLM engine integration, model management (ModelDownloader, MODEL_ALIASES), WASM memory management

ADR-007 success metrics target ~95% capability coverage, ACID + Cypher graph consistency, browser vector DB via WASM, full RAG via RLM, kernel embedding making RVF an "active compute container".

Per ADR-0177's Load-bearing finding #5 — refined 2026-05-12 with a deliberate upstream-rationale audit:

Search Result
factory.ts references to SelfLearningRvfBackend / SelfLearningConfig Zero. No TODO, FIXME, "disabled", "opt-in", "future", or env-var-gating comment near the return statement.
grep -rn 'SelfLearningRvfBackend' src/ excluding the file itself Zero matches anywhere — not in factory, not in tests, not in index.ts public exports, not in CLI. Built but never even surfaced as a public API.
git log src/backends/factory.ts Single commit 8b3388b "init: agentdb package source + marketing UI". Entire agentdb codebase landed as one initial dump. No subsequent commit refines the factory's return choice — no commit narrative explains the orphan.
SelfLearningRvfBackend.ts header docstring Plain class description. No "not yet default" caveat.
ADR-006 SelfLearningConfig definition (line ~480) learning?: boolean (default: true) — the ADR explicitly designs the wrapper to be default-on. Factory.ts contradicts the ADR's own design.
ADR-006 status field "Proposed" since 2026-02-17. Not Accepted. Three months elapsed without status flip.
ADR-006 "Negative" + "Risks" sections Enumerate construction costs (~0.7ms latency, async factory + WASM load, memory growth, learning instability, cold start) and pre-mitigate them via "conservative defaults — learning is additive, never degrades below baseline RvfBackend performance." Not framed as reasons to orphan; framed as costs the ADR accepts.

The honest read (not "they forgot")

ADR-005 (which CREATED the 6 components) is Accepted — 100% per the audit. ADR-006 (which WIRES them into RvfBackend via the wrapper) is Proposed — never accepted. The wrapper code per ADR-006's design landed in the dump commit alongside everything else. The factory.ts change that would deliver ADR-006's default: true mandate — a one-line return-flip — was never made, presumably because ADR-006 hasn't been accepted yet. Three months elapsed (2026-02-17 → 2026-05-12) without the status flip. There is no upstream PR proposing the factory change.

This is an unfinished governance handoff, not a designed-and-justified opt-in. It's not "we built it but decided not to ship it" — there's no design rationale anywhere for that decision. It's "we built it but the ADR that authorises it is still in draft." The codebase is essentially in a "design implemented, awaiting governance acceptance" state — but governance never moved.

Prior framing (now superseded, kept for traceability)

ADR-0177's earlier draft hypothesised: "ADR-006's orphaned wrapper is the kind of bug that won't surface in upstream because nobody's deploying production agents on npm i agentdb. Fork's bundle-release posture would surface this immediately — and the fix is trivial. This is exactly the value upstream's compat envelope blocks: upstream can't flip the factory default without breaking dual-mode-fallback semantics their existing users depend on. Fork can."

The 2026-05-12 source audit refuted this. The "compat envelope" claim wasn't backed by any specific dual-mode-fallback semantic that would actually break — it was a guess at upstream's reasoning, not a finding. The simpler evidence-based read is: ADR-006 hasn't been accepted, so nobody's pulled the lever.

The fork already pulled the lever

Fork's ADR-0177 Phase 2 implements the one-line factory change:

  • Where: forks/agentdb/src/backends/factory.ts:166
  • Diff: type import for SelfLearningConfig, factory body swap to SelfLearningRvfBackend.create(), comment update citing ADR-006 + ADR-0177 Phase 2.
  • Status: ✅ Landed 2026-05-12 in commit 511b7d3. One commit ahead of upstream HEAD a478ab3.
  • Why we don't PR it back: memory feedback-no-upstream-donate-backs retired the original Phase 7 (upstream PR) — fork improvements stay fork-only. The fork's @sparkleideas/agentdb delivers the README's "+36% from feedback alone" claim that npm i agentdb from upstream does not.
  • Pending verification: npm run release acceptance pass + Phase 2 NDCG@10 benchmark (target: ≥10% improvement vs static HNSW as proof-of-loop; +36% is the long-training upstream claim).

sql.js is a HARD dependency upstream (every install pulls it). The cascade serves restricted-host populations (browsers, Lambda, environments without native bindings). For typical npm-install users on standard Node.js, the runtime path is RVF + native HNSW — same as the fork's memory_* axis.

2.4 Upstream MCP surface today

Both memory_* AND agentdb_* tool families ship in upstream (verified against ruvnet/ruflo/v3/@claude-flow/cli/src/mcp-tools/agentdb-tools.ts). The 18 agentdb_* tools include: agentdb_health, agentdb_controllers, agentdb_hierarchical-store/-recall/-delete, agentdb_session-start/-end, agentdb_causal-edge/-edge-delete/-node-delete, agentdb_pattern-store/-search, agentdb_feedback, agentdb_consolidate, agentdb_route, agentdb_semantic-route, agentdb_context-synthesize, agentdb_batch.

All 18 route through memory-bridge.ts (lines 48-54: let bridgeModule = await import('../memory/memory-bridge.js')) — which is upstream's coordination layer between the MCP tools and the AgentDB controllers. The handlers call bridgeStoreEntry(), bridgeHierarchicalStore(), etc., and the bridge writes the actual data into .swarm/memory.db.

So upstream's MCP surface has been TWO families since ADR-0053 (2026-02-25). The fork didn't add the agentdb_* namespace — it inherited it. Earlier drafts of this document were wrong on that point.

What's distinctive in upstream's current state:

  • Both surfaces route through one bridge module.
  • Both surfaces ultimately write to one file (.swarm/memory.db).
  • The bridge can coordinate cross-surface operations (e.g. record an attestation for a memory_store write and a pattern-store in one logical step).
  • ADR-007 Phase 6 lists 7 additional agentdb_rvf_* MCP tools as proposed but 0% implemented per the audit — would extend the surface further.

2.5 What's stopping the fork from completing the upstream vision?

Upstream's documented vision is 95% capability coverage by the end of ADR-007's 5-phase roadmap. The 9-agent audit measured upstream at **60% aggregate**. The fork inherits this baseline. So the gap is ~35 percentage points. What does that 35% consist of, and which parts are actually blocking?

Bucket A: Easy wins (~5% of gap, fork-doable in days)

Gap Source Effort
init --backend rvf wizard ADR-003 Phase 4 (0%) ~0.5 day
7 agentdb_rvf_* MCP tools ADR-003 Phase 6 (0%) ~1-2 days

Full RvfMigrator with detect / .bak / dry-run streaming ADR-003 Phase 3 (partial) ~1 day
3 missing ADR-006 SoTA enhancements (DPO loss, NV-Retriever false-negative filter, SCAFFOLD/K-Merge federation) ADR-006 extensions ~1-2 days

Total ~5-7 person-days. These are stopped by engineering priority, not by any technical blocker — they're below the line of value vs. fork's actual user-facing work.

Bucket B: Big features (~20% of gap, multi-week scope each)

Gap Source Comment

Full model import/export pipeline (SafeTensors/HF/JSON/Binary) ADR-007 Phase 2 + 5 Touches model lifecycle, not fork's core path
Streaming token generation + streaming graph queries (QueryResultStream, HyperedgeStream, NodeStream) ADR-007 Phase 4 (5%) Largest single gap; speculative value for fork's MCP-tool consumers
Hyperbolic attention (DualSpaceAttention) ADR-007 Phase 4 Research-grade; CLI scaffolding exists but compute is JS simulation per ADR-002 audit (22% real)
RuvLLM engine integration (NativeRuvLLM.RuvLLMEngine) ADR-007 Phase 5 (25%) Lazy-loaded entry point exists; full integration is multi-week

8 of ADR-002 "New Files" that don't exist (CurriculumLearner, NegativeMiner, ContrastiveLearner, FastGRNNRouter, HyperbolicSpace, DualSpaceSearcher, AdaptiveTensorStore, TemporalHyperedgeStore) ADR-002 (22%) Replacing JS simulations with native code; not blocking fork's hot path

These are stopped by scope vs. engineering investment. None are technically impossible — they're just real systems work that the fork pays for only if a feature earns its keep against the fork's actual MCP-tool consumers (skills, agents, plugins).

Bucket C: Upstream-only or undefined (~10% of gap, not fork-completable)

Gap Source Why fork can't complete it
@agentdb/chat package (SvelteKit + RVF kernel embedding chat UI) ADR-008 (0%) Doesn't exist anywhere. @agentdb/chat serve claim in upstream README is misattributed (audit finding). No prerequisites met. Outside fork's MCP-tool-shape goals.
Causal Atlas RVF Runtime ADR-009 (0%) The file is a 6-byte placeholder containing the literal text "i weds". No frontmatter, no Status, no Date, no Decision, no enumerated artifacts. We literally have no design to implement. Pre-existing causal stack (CausalMemoryGraph.ts 875 LoC) is unrelated prior work — not ADR-009 implementation.
ADR-006 status flip from "Proposed" → "Accepted" Upstream governance Fork can't move upstream's ADR status field. We've already worked around it locally (factory flip in fork commit 511b7d3); the upstream-side resolution requires upstream's maintainer to accept the ADR.
"Future @ruvector PostgreSQL extension that reads/writes .rvf segments directly" ADR-006 names it as future work Doesn't exist; no upstream PR proposes it; building it is a multi-month research project. Outside fork scope (and would require Rust + postgres extension work).

Summary

So when the audit says "~60% aggregate," that's not a single block of "stuff we haven't done." It's a layered story:

  • ~5% engineering priority (fork could do it; chooses to spend the time on user-facing work instead).
  • 20% scope vs. value (real systems work; fork picks high-value pieces when they earn it — e.g. the ADR-0174 Phase A.5 narrow Cypher executor patch is ready as `1KLoC Rust`).
  • ~10% structural impossibility (upstream artifacts that don't exist or aren't designed).

What the fork has already done with this gap:

  • Phase 1: Reverted divergent ADR-0170/0174/0175 substrate work to align with upstream's RVF-first vision (per ADR-0177). Done.
  • Phase 2: Factory flip for SelfLearningRvfBackend (commit 511b7d3). Done. Pending verification.
  • Phase 3: Cypher executor patch in forks/ruvector/crates/ruvector-graph/src/executor/mod.rs:129. Ready (~1KLoC Rust).
  • Phase 4-5: Track upstream's ADR-007 Phases 2-5 opportunistically; invest where the feature earns its keep.
  • Phase 6: Retire fork's ruvector-bridge.ts plugin (pgvector via pg.Pool, violates ADR-006's no-pgvector mandate).

The 35-pp gap is paced by engineering economics + governance + structural impossibility — not by knowledge gaps. The fork knows what upstream intended; it has source-audited what upstream shipped; the remaining work is doing or not doing each piece on its own merits.

3. Fork architecture today (sparkling/main)

3.1 What the fork ships

Three architectural moves diverged the fork from upstream:

  • ADR-0086 (2026-04-14) — replaced sql.js with RVF (@ruvector/rvf-node) as the primary substrate for memory_*. Titled "Single Storage Abstraction (RVF-First)" — intended to unify on one substrate. Failed at "Debt 15 ControllerRegistry dual-backend" because the 10+ neural controllers need relational schemas RVF cannot host.
  • ADR-0085 (2026-04-13) — deleted memory-bridge.ts (~3,650 lines). The cross-cutting coordination layer became collateral. ADR-0179 round-1 found 6 features lost.
  • ADR-0112 (2026-05-01) — formalized Debt 15 as deliberate architecture: "two independent stores, feature-aligned." Introduced the agentdb_* MCP surface as a peer of memory_*.

The result: two MCP surfaces, two files on disk, two failure modes. ADR-0177 (proposed 2026-05-12) supersedes ADR-0170/0174/0175 and proposes pivoting back to upstream's RVF-first single-surface vision.

3.2 Fork MCP surfaces — for reference compare against §1 (upstream intention) and §2 (upstream today)

Two tool families:

  • memory_* (RVF axis) — memory_store, memory_search, memory_retrieve, memory_delete, memory_list. All writes go to .claude-flow/memory.rvf.
  • agentdb_* (AgentDB SQLite axis) — agentdb_hierarchical-store/recall/query/delete, agentdb_causal-edge/-query/-recall, agentdb_session_start/end, agentdb_route, agentdb_batch, agentdb_context_synthesize, agentdb_health, plus controller-specific tools (~50 tools total). All writes go to .swarm/memory.db.

ADR-0112 forbids any MCP tool from spanning both. The caller picks the axis at design time. Upstream has no equivalent of agentdb_* in either intention or current shipped state.

3.7 The detail that matters most — AgentDB is itself internally hybrid

A point the devil's advocate kept hammering: regardless of the surface architecture, AgentDB v3 internally already has both SQLite and a native vector index. The "single axis" question is really about whether the fork also keeps a separate top-level vector substrate (RVF) or relies on AgentDB's internal one.

Implications:

  • The "dual substrate" the fork is debating already exists inside AgentDB. Reflexion stores its episode rows in SQLite and its episode embeddings in the native HNSW backend — two substrates, one controller, one MCP tool call.
  • Option Z (single surface, dual substrate internal) is, structurally, what AgentDB already is — one API, internally hybrid. Adopting Z at the fork level is consistent with how the controllers below already work.
  • The fork's RVF substrate at the memory_* axis adds a third storage primitive on top of AgentDB's two. Whether that third primitive earns its keep is the real perf question — and depends on whether RVF (purpose-built single-file vector substrate) outperforms AgentDB's own vector layer enough to justify the operational cost.

5. Pros and cons

5.1 Upstream single-axis (intention + today)

Pros:

  • One file, one backup, one restore point. No coordination needed across substrates. Point-in-time restore is trivial.
  • One MCP surface. Callers don't pick axis; agents have less context to manage; LLMs see one tool family.
  • One audit chokepoint. MutationGuard / AttestationLog / TieredCache wire into one place. The bridge's deletion didn't lose features under this model because there was a coherent integration layer to delete.
  • Cross-store transactions are possible. A skill record and its embedding can land atomically.
  • Aligned with upstream design intent. ADR-006/009 are stable; minimal architectural churn.

Cons:

  • Vector search is slow on the runtime path. sql.js cosine over rehydrated JSON embeddings is ~10-100× slower than native HNSW for typical workloads.
  • One failure mode. SQLite corruption or WAL stall affects everything.
  • HybridBackend exists but isn't used. The design is bypassed at runtime; the canonical CLI path is the worst of the three ADR-006 options.
  • Workload mismatch. Relational neural-controller data and K/V vector data share one substrate's invariants — typically SQLite's, which over-serves vectors and under-serves their access patterns.

5.2 Fork dual-axis (ADR-0086/0112)

Pros:

  • Workload-correct substrate per axis. RVF for vector-dominant K/V; SQLite for relational neural controllers. Each substrate's invariants match its workload.
  • Native HNSW on the vector hot path. 2-3× faster than AgentDB's internal HNSW; 5-50× faster than upstream's sql.js path.
  • Independent failure modes. RVF corruption doesn't take out neural controllers; SQLite lock contention doesn't stall vector recall.
  • Phase C.3 cold-start optimization. memory_* axis doesn't pay registry-bootstrap cost; only agentdb_* does.
  • Explicit semantics at the tool surface. memory_store vs agentdb_hierarchical-store makes the contract decision visible at call time.

Cons:

  • Two of everything. Two files, two backups, two restore paths, two audit streams, two MCP namespaces, two init paths, two failure modes to monitor.
  • Cross-cutting features have no home. MutationGuard, AttestationLog, hybrid BM25+semantic, ExplainableRecall — none fit cleanly on either axis. Round 1's lost features are direct evidence.
  • Cross-store transactions forbidden by design. ADR-0112 explicitly forbids them. Any feature needing K/V + vector + relational coherence cannot be built.
  • Cross-axis audit correlation is impossible. Incident response cannot reconstruct an attacker's full footprint from one query.
  • 9+ ADRs of architectural churn. 0086, 0090, 0112, 0154, 0161, 0164, 0166, 0178, 0179 all trace to the dual-substrate reality.
  • ADR-0086 title is a misrepresentation. "Single Storage Abstraction" delivered dual storage; the title was never updated.
  • The "150-12,500× speedup" claim is dishonest. Comparison is RVF NAPI HNSW vs sql.js JSON cosine; honest comparator is AgentDB native HNSW with 2-3× gap. Status-quo-defender conceded this in the round-2 council.
  • Upstream sync drift compounds. agentdb_* is purely fork-additions with no upstream signal to merge against.
  • Cognitive tax on every new feature. Every controller, every MCP tool, every plugin has to decide which axis at design time.

Reading the matrix: upstream's intended architecture (UI) is the goal. Upstream today (UT) is off-target because of the orphaned wrapper. The fork started from UT, added a second surface to escape sql.js perf (FT), then accumulated the dual-axis tax. ADR-0177 + Option Z converge on a single architecture (one surface, RVF-primary, dual-substrate internal) that closes the gap to UI without giving back fork's perf wins.

Positions are illustrative, not measured. Y-axis position depends on workload (hot vector loops vs casual use); X-axis position depends on whether you count CI/backup tooling burden or just runtime cost. The relative ordering reflects round-2 council consensus; absolute positions would require running benchmarks the council flagged as a pre-flight requirement.

The "best of both" quadrant is the architecture nobody currently ships — single user surface (upstream-shaped, low ops cost) with dual substrate internally (fork-shaped, high perf). This is Option Z from the round-2 council deliberation.

6. How we got here — architectural evolution

The fork's dual axis didn't emerge from a single decision. It accumulated across four months of ADR-by-ADR moves, each locally justified, that composed into the current state.

The pattern visible across this timeline:

  • ADR-0053 intended a single-CLI-surface architecture with the bridge as the cross-cutting integration layer.
  • ADR-0084 → ADR-0085 removed the bridge as redundant (true structurally), losing its cross-cutting features (collateral, not yet noticed).
  • ADR-0086 intended a single substrate (RVF-First); failed at Debt 15; accepted a dual-substrate residue.
  • ADR-0112 promoted the accepted residue from "internal substrate detail" to "deliberate dual MCP surface."
  • ADR-0179 (round 1) discovered the deletion cost. Round 2 discovered the dual-surface cost.

Each ADR was locally correct. The composition is what produced the current tax.

7. What the bridge did — and what got lost when it died

memory-bridge.ts was ADR-0053's "Phase 1 Foundation." It wasn't just a wrapper — it was the single chokepoint where cross-cutting concerns (policy, audit, cache, fusion) attached to every write and read.

When ADR-0085 deleted the bridge module, all six middleware concerns went with it. The fork's dual axis then made re-wiring them harder, because each is cross-cutting — they apply to mutations regardless of substrate. Under upstream's single axis, each had ONE call site to live at. Under the fork's dual axis, each needs TWO call sites (or a shared middleware module imported by both routers).

ADR-0179 is the proposed restoration; ADR-0179 round-1 council ratified 6-B-amended (axis-correct call-site restoration with shared middleware). The bridge does not return; the features do.

8.5 Round-3 council findings (2026-05-13)

After round-2 endorsed Option Z (substrate collapse + ADR-0112 revert), round-3 deliberated three follow-up questions and surfaced three load-bearing findings that materially refine the recommendation.

Bombshell 1: upstream's bridge is a half-finished chokepoint

Security-judge body-diffed memory-bridge.ts HEAD ef73a1616 and found MutationGuard + AttestationLog wired into only 5 of 13 mutation paths:

  • Guarded: bridgeStoreEntry, bridgeDeleteEntry, bridgeDeleteHierarchical, bridgeDeleteCausalEdge, bridgeDeleteCausalNode.
  • Unguarded (write operations on more state-sensitive controllers): bridgeHierarchicalStore (direct hm.store(...)), bridgeBatchOperation, bridgeRecordCausalEdge (asymmetric — DELETE is guarded but CREATE isn't), bridgeConsolidate, bridgeSessionStart/End/RouteTask, bridgeAddToHNSW, fast-path of bridgeStorePattern, fanout in bridgeRecordFeedback.

Implication: restoring the bridge "as upstream has it" reproduces an incomplete chokepoint that LOOKS complete. The half-finished chokepoint is the most dangerous shape because it stops the next refactor asking "where else?" — the answer looks like "the bridge handles it" when 8 of 13 paths are unguarded.

Bombshell 2: ADR-0177's RVF-only target is operationally impossible

Memory-judge found the 10+ AgentDB controllers (reflexionMemory, causalGraph, skillLibrary, learningSystem, etc.) have FK-structured relational schemas (episode_embeddings.episode_id → episodes.id, causal edges between nodes, etc.). RVF is K/V + vector with no JOIN, no WHERE table_x.fk = table_y.id, no transactional multi-row mutation. You cannot straightforwardly re-point these controllers to RvfBackend.

Three options:

  • A) Denormalise into RVF blobs — collapse relations into one K/V record per logical entity. Loses query-by-FK.
  • B) Hybrid: RVF for vectors, SQLite for relational FK structure — what ADR-0177's "SQLite as fallback when explicitly needed" actually means in practice. It's a permanent dual-substrate operating mode, not a fallback.
  • C) Replace controllers' implementations entirely as RVF-native. Multi-quarter effort.

ADR-0177 most plausibly means option B with possibly A for some controllers. The realistic target is RVF + SQLite hybrid forever, with per-controller System-of-Record (SoR) assignment: SoR-authoritative + materialised-view-best-effort + periodic orphan-sweeper. No two-phase commit. ADR-0180 needs to make this honest.

Bombshell 3: bridgeRecordFeedback 3-4× silent storage amplification

Perf-judge traced bridgeRecordFeedback: every feedback event writes to learningSystem AND reasoningBank AND skills (if quality≥0.9 in loop) AND unconditionally to bridgeStoreEntry's SQL path. No dedup. Storage amplification factor: ~3-4× per feedback event. Invisible in the API but very visible in disk usage under heavy hooks_post-task workload. If we restore the bridge as-is, the amplification comes with it. ADR-0179's restoration must include dedup at the feedback path.

Mid-round framing reframe + post-reframe convergence

Mid-session, the user reframed the deliberation: "These discussions are for determining the direction. We have contradicting ADRs. Once we have found the answer, we can clean it up. See the old ADRs as exploration, and inputs to our decision." Experts were instructed to argue from forward-design lessons, not constraint-preservation.

The reframe produced sharper convergence than the initial 4/2/1/1 raw vote suggested.

Post-reframe vote: 3 bridge-shape / 3 middleware-shape / 1 hybrid / 1 opposition. But 7-of-7 voting members agree on the underlying architecture:

  1. One thin coordinator (~500-1000 LoC, NOT 2,370) at the MCP-tool-dispatch boundary.
  2. Cross-cutting middleware applied uniformly there: MutationGuard / AttestationLog / TieredCache / BM25 fusion / ExplainableRecall provenance / SkillLibrary auto-promotion (with dedup to fix the 3-4× amplification).
  3. Type-level enforcement via branded types + required MutationContext argument — closes upstream's half-finished chokepoint gap (5 of 13 → 13 of 13 mutation paths guarded). This is stronger than upstream's bridge, not just structurally equivalent.
  4. Substrate: RVF-primary with documented PERMANENT_SQLITE carve-outs. Hybrid forever, not transitional. Per-controller System-of-Record assignment.
  5. Both MCP surfaces preserved (memory_* + agentdb_*). Parallel evolution with upstream.
  6. Controllers own their internal multi-table transactions. Coordinator dispatches; controllers own FK consistency.
  7. ADR-0112 retired — drop the no-cross-surface-coordination rule.
  8. Lazy-per-tool init.
  9. Single audit chain above the substrate split; substrate is a record-property, not identity.
  10. +36% wrapper fix lands at the coordinator as a single insertion point.

The residual disagreement is naming, not architecture

  • "Bridge" camp (bridge-defender, memory-judge, integration-judge): name it controller-bridge.ts, line-level structural homology with upstream's memory-bridge.ts for merge alignment.
  • "Middleware" camp (status-quo-defender, security-judge, perf-judge weakly): name it src/memory/middleware/, type-level enforcement explicit in file structure (registerMutationHandler<T> factory + branded GuardedWrite<T> types).

These are not architecturally different objects. A "thin bridge module that applies typed middleware via HOF" and "a middleware module that registers handlers via a typed factory" are the same shape. The naming dispute is residual; the engineering decision is settled.

Per memory-judge's load-bearing observation: "The bridge isn't axis-shaped — it's a dispatcher with middleware. Round-2's axis framing collapses under the bridge frame." And per perf-judge: "The router-shim form of middleware IS the bridge with worse vocabulary."

Synthesized forward direction

A thin coordinator (~500-1000 LoC, not 2,370) at the MCP-tool-dispatch boundary, applying cross-cutting middleware via type-enforced wrappers + controller-method backstop:

  • MutationGuard via registerMutationHandler<TArgs, TResult> factory + branded GuardedWrite<T> types — compiler refuses any handler that calls controller.store(rawArgs) without going through the factory. All 13+ mutation paths guarded, not 5 of 13. Closes upstream's half-finished gap.
  • AttestationLog as separate attestation.db file (retained per upstream's pattern — append-only audit on a compacting vector store would be wrong). Single audit chain regardless of substrate; substrate is a record-property.
  • Controller method backstop (security-judge's P3): controllers' write methods require a MutationContext argument. Throw fatal if missing per feedback-no-fallbacks. Defends against controller-direct callers that bypass the MCP surface.
  • TieredCache read-side cache layer with invalidation bound to MutationGuard.
  • BM25 + semantic fusion as default for search.
  • ExplainableRecall provenance attached to every result.
  • SkillLibrary promotion via coordinator call on feedback events (with dedup to fix the 3-4× amplification).

Drop (from upstream's 2,370 LoC): registry indirection (ADR-0084 resolves at handler), direct SQL writes (controllers own their writes), HNSW-singleton dynamic-import dances, the 60+ unused upstream exports. This is why the proposed shape is ~500-1000 LoC instead of 2,370.

Migration window (Regime A): try-RVF-then-fall-back, bounded by 7-day deadline, sweeper job for orphan eviction, anchor-attestation record bridging old-chain to new-chain.

Naming choice (residual): call it controller-bridge.ts (bridge camp) or src/memory/middleware/ (middleware camp). Either is honest; both implement the same thing. A neutral third option is controller-router.ts or controller-coordinator.ts — captures both instincts. The naming dispute doesn't affect what gets built.

9. Open questions and unknowns

The round-2 devil's advocate flagged that two pre-flight artifacts must exist before any X/Y/Z vote is meaningful:

  1. The honest perf benchmark has not been run. RVF NAPI HNSW vs AgentDB's own native HNSW on representative fork workload — insert, k-NN search, k-NN with metadata JOIN, cold start. Without this measurement, every option is being evaluated against a phantom baseline. Round-2 perf-judge estimated 2-3× but flagged this is reasoned from code paths, not measured.
  2. ADR-0086's Status section has not been amended to acknowledge Debt 15 as a partial unification failure. Currently the ADR title says "Single Storage Abstraction (RVF-First)" while the outcome is dual-storage. Until ADR-0086 is honest about what it delivered vs intended, decisions referencing it inherit the mismatch.

Other unverified claims in this document:

  • The "3-10ms" / "8-25ms" cold-start estimates are reasoned from file-open + WAL-init costs on macOS/SSD; not measured on the fork's test corpus.
  • The "~50 agentdb_* tools" count is approximate; the actual count varies by enabled controllers per agentdb_health.
  • The "9+ ADRs of axis-related decisions" is the count of ADRs that explicitly cite the axis as load-bearing; the actual touchpoint count across all ADRs is higher.
